content.title: What is a Queue?
content.description: A Queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle, where the first element inserted is the first one removed.

content.content: A Queue works similarly to a line of people waiting at a ticket counter. The person who arrives first gets served first. This behavior makes Queues extremely useful in scheduling, resource management, operating systems, networking, and real-time systems.

content.title: Key Principle
content.content: Queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out), unlike Stack which follows LIFO (Last In, First Out).
Many real-world systems process tasks in the order they arrive. Queues help ensure fairness and maintain the correct processing sequence.

content.title: Think Like a Queue
content.description: The earliest element entering the queue always leaves first.

content.content:
A Queue has two important pointers:

  • Front → Points to the first element.
  • Rear → Points to the last element.

content.title: Important Terms
content.content: Insertion happens at the Rear, while deletion happens at the Front.

items.question: Enqueue
items.answer: Insert an element at the rear of the queue.

items.question: Dequeue
items.answer: Remove an element from the front of the queue.

items.question: Front
items.answer: View the first element without removing it.

items.question: isEmpty
items.answer: Check whether the queue contains elements.

content.content: Enqueue adds a new element to the rear of the queue.
Dequeue removes the oldest element from the front of the queue.

content.title: Observation
content.content: Elements always leave in the same order they entered.

items.question: CPU Scheduling
items.answer: Operating systems schedule processes using queues.

items.question: Printer Management
items.answer: Print jobs wait in a queue.

items.question: Customer Service Systems
items.answer: Customers are served in arrival order.

items.question: Task Scheduling
items.answer: Jobs wait until resources become available.

items.question: Fair Processing
items.answer: Tasks are handled in arrival order.

items.question: Widely Applicable
items.answer: Used across software and hardware systems.

items.question: Queue Overflow
items.answer: Occurs when inserting into a full queue.

items.question: Queue Underflow
items.answer: Occurs when removing from an empty queue.

items.question: Confusing FIFO and LIFO
items.answer: Queue follows FIFO, Stack follows LIFO.

content.title: Interview Tip
content.content: When you see problems involving processing tasks in arrival order, scheduling, buffering, or waiting lines, think about Queue as a possible solution.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Many advanced structures such as Circular Queue, Deque, Priority Queue, and BFS traversal are built on top of Queue fundamentals.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Queues are widely used in scheduling.
Operating systems heavily rely on queues.
Queue is one of the most important linear data structures.
